articles.title: University of California
articles.author: Joe Mathews
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Do you have a brilliant child who makes you proud—but is also a pain in the butt? So does the Golden State. Its great, infuriating child is the University of California. In her terrific new book, California Dreams: The Making and Remaking of the University of California , journalist and author Miriam Pawel (my former L.A. Times colleague) tags all the bases of UC history, from the university’s 1868 founding in the Berkeley Hills through its expansion into a $60 billion educational and economic engine encompassing 10 campuses, six health systems, and three national laboratories. But the book is really something more intimate: an examination of the fraught, familial relationship between our state and its world-class university system. Pawel tells the stories of university graduates, including UC system presidents Robert Sproul and Clark Kerr and (most wonderfully, for this reader) Kenneth Bailey, a pioneer in teacher education who was an important figure in the history of two different UC campuses. She also conveys the stories of its campuses, with heavy emphasis on Berkeley and, unexpectedly, UC Irvine, to which this book is an extended love letter. Related: The African Democracy That Makes Presidents Sit Down and Listen California Dreams is often quite moving, as it shows how the university shaped the ideas, ambitions, and people of California. Among the book’s stars are the acclaimed farmer and writer David Mas Masumoto, who has become an important civic figure in the Central Valley. Many of Pawel’s most memorable stories are told through the life of Milicent Washburn Shinn, a pioneer in the field of child psychology. She was one of 43 members of Berkeley’s undergraduate class of 1880, and became the first woman to receive a PhD from the university. The book chronologically charts the shifting arguments that Californians have had with each other about what they want their university to be. As the UC grew into arguably the world’s finest public university system, each new generation of institutional leaders feared that something has been lost. Each new generation of politicians fought with the university. And each new generation of students complained that the university is lacking. All the arguing is the result of this fact: the UC is one of the few institutions important and interesting enough to connect all of California’s places and people. “In a state larger and more diverse in all aspects than many countries,” Pawel writes, “the University remained one of the few forces that transcended disparate regions and groups. It was perhaps the only public institution that inspired widespread loyalty and admiration, even among those who were rejected.” In this context, present-day Californians’ constant disputes about the UC are reassuring—proof that the university still matters. Today’s fights—over “woke” politics, diversity, and the current ban on using SAT scores in admissions—seem familiar, and less divisive, when compared to the past. Pawel recounts how, during the Red Scare of the 1950s, the UC and its Board of Regents engaged in brutal ideological purges that make 21st-century cancellations look tame. At one point, all faculty were required to sign an anti-communist loyalty oath. World-renowned scholars who refused were fired or walked away in protest, fracturing the faculty until courts intervened. Related: Gavin Newsom's Gubernatorial Legacy and What's Coming for California Long before current debates over campus free speech or political interference, the UC found itself in a vise, squeezed between Free Speech Movement student radicals and a conservative public outraged by campus disruption. The anti-UC fury propelled Ronald Reagan into the governor’s mansion in 1967, where he engineered the firing of the university’s president, Clark Kerr, creator of California’s 1960 Master Plan for Higher Education. And in the 1990s, the UC was the central front in a statewide battle over affirmative action that ran even hotter than the DEI debates of today. That battle included a voter-approved measure in 1996 to ban the practice. That ban, in turn, reduced diversity throughout a system that was nowhere close to reflecting California demographics back then, and still lags in diversity today. One reason why the UC has remained so controversial is that it is expected to do two contradictory things. First, it’s supposed to be exclusive. The UC screens the population of California (and the rest of the world) to identify, admit, and educate the most promising students; what Kerr called an “aristocracy of talent.” At the same time, the university is supposed to be inclusive, equity-producing engine of social mobility in a very unequal state of 40 million people. The distance between UC exclusion and inclusion is illustrated every spring, when Berkeley forms a freshman class of less than 7,000 students from a pool of more than 130,000 applications. The book suggests that the UC’s true superpower is its resilience—its ability to survive, absorb conflict, and adapt. At least so far. Pawel does not reckon with how the UC’s success has made it the target of multiple threats from a hostile Trump administration, which uses the leverage of federal funding to demand the reversal of more progressive policies. Related: Recyclables for Rice: Initiatives to Help Planet and People Near the book’s end, Pawel recounts a speech that writer Joan Didion, Berkeley Class of ’56, gave at the university’s 125th anniversary celebration in 1993. Didion talked about growing up in the once-small town of Sacramento, when the state was less rich, less educated, and less global. “That California doesn’t exist anymore,” Didion said. “We joined the rest of the country, the rest of the world. We wrenched ourselves from our provincial Eden into history, and as we did so, some of us kicking and screaming, this university did what it has been doing for 125 years now. It provided the bridge. It provided the forum. It provided the safe house in which old and new California could be seen to be not irreconcilable.” Indeed, California, old and new, has grown together with its university. Today, the state and the campuses, paradoxically, are growing more open and diverse at the same time they grow more expensive and exclusive. Perhaps California and the UC fight for the same reason parents fight with children: because they’re related, they’re too much alike. Zócalo Public Square

articles.title: Jewish Identity
articles.author: H. Scott Prosterman
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. On December 11, 2019, convicted felon Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13899 , which declared Judaism to be a separate “race” and “ethnicity;” and all Jews of common “national origin.” The purpose was to twist Title VI of the 1964 Civil Rights Act into a tool for speech suppression. It had the “hat trick” effect of patronizing Jews and persecuting Palestinians; and prosecuting an attack on free speech. Indirectly, this was a misappropriation of the Civil Rights Act, and it also undermines the prospects for a two-state solution between Israel and Palestinians. Despite 1000 years of pogroms, culminating with the Holocaust, most Jews have resisted being categorized as a specific race. Jews are known to be in 99 countries, spanning the full spectrum of human ethnicity. Judaism is a religion and a culture of shared ancestry. Many non-observant Jews are fiercely proud of their culture and heritage, as well as taking a deep pride in Jewish humor ; and our accomplishments in the entertainment industries, financial sectors and academia. Iconic athletes such as Sandy Koufax, Mark Spitz and Deni Avdija are also part of that equation. Judaism is not a race, nor a nationality outside of Israel. But globally, fewer Jews identify with Israel than any time since its founding. As for Israel, a recent AP/NORC opinion poll found that “for many U.S. Jews, support for Israel remains a bedrock of their religious identity, its existence a guarantee of Jewish self-determination and safety.” Yet it found profound discomfort with the policies of the extreme-right government of Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud Party, which many feel has perverted Zionism into a genocidal ideology that is an anathema to its founding ideals. Author Rich Forer and others argue, however, that “ethnic cleansing and genocide are the inevitable culmination of the Zionist project.” Related: 9/11 and Fear Mongering in 2026 Among Jews who are religious, about 70% of the American community, the poll discovered that around half see Israel’s actions in Gaza as unjustified, and 25% are willing to characterize them as genocidal. About a third of U.S. Jews are not religiously observant, and fully 40 percent of this group agrees that Israel committed a genocide in Gaza. Only six percent of these secular-minded American Jews identify as Zionists. Three-quarters of non-religious Jews say that they are “not too” or “not at all” emotionally attached to Israel. David Crary and his colleagues at AP write , “Anna Constant, 56, of Seattle identifies as culturally Jewish and says she doesn’t feel closely connected to Israel. ‘I kind of think of myself as an American version of a Jew. I do have a homeland,’ she said, referring to the United States.” Ms. Constant has been recategorized by Donald Trump as having a separate race and identity, whether she likes it or not. The Likud Party under PM Benjamin Netanyahu has generated more anti-Semitism than any dynamic since WWII . While illegal settlements have been built in the West Bank during the tenure of every Israeli prime minister since 1967, Netanyahu’s agenda has been a steroid-fueled explosion of settlements, with a blind eye toward squatter violence. Related: Gloria Steinem Gave Women Permission to Choose The increasing rightward shift of Zionism and Israel has transformed the notion of “liberal Zionism” into an oxymoronic anachronism for those still holding on. American and Israeli Jews, along with Christian Zionists, are notorious for supporting human rights for all people, except Palestinians. I once heard the great singer Mary Travis essentially say that “the hammer of justice and bell of freedom” applies to everyone in the world, except Palestinians. When I spoke to her after her talk to a Zionist group in Memphis, she didn’t back down. Trump issued that Executive Order two days after he had told the America-Israel Council, “You’re brutal killers; you’re not nice people, but you have to vote for me; you have no choice . . .” The context was the alarming rise of anti-Semitism as a result of the failure to distinguish Judaism, the religion; from Zionism, the political ideology. Worldwide, Jews are being unfairly demonized for the sins of Netanyahu’s Likud Party, which has prosecuted genocide in Gaza, as a diversion from the pogroms in the West Bank . Informed Comment

articles.title: Charity Begins at Home
articles.author: Eva Amar
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. October is Domestic Violence Awareness Month, a time to recognize victims, honor survivors, and acknowledge the people and organizations that help them escape abuse. It is also an appropriate time to examine how organizations entrusted with protecting vulnerable people spend their resources. According to an October 13 investigation by the Los Angeles Times, 1736 Family Crisis Center, a Southern California nonprofit that receives nearly 94 percent of its revenue from government grants, provides its CEO, Carol Adelkoff, with a luxury Santa Monica apartment costing approximately $6,500 a month and a leased BMW for her use in Hawaii, where she maintains her primary residence. For an organization whose mission includes providing shelter to people who have nowhere safe to live, the arrangement presents an irony that's difficult to ignore. 1736 Family Crisis Center operates six shelters and provides counseling, legal assistance, crisis intervention, and other services. It reports serving nearly 11,000 individuals annually through direct services, including more than 4,600 children and youth. Those numbers include far more than shelter residents, but they illustrate the importance of the organization's work. Its IRS Form 990 for the fiscal year ending June 2025 reports $15,442,080 in revenue, including $14,507,714 in government grants, and $15,504,340 in expenses. The organization spent $62,260 more than it received. Those are public dollars supporting a mission that deserves public accountability. Related: Don't Look Down: America's Democracy Is Under Strain—and the World Is Watching The Women Behind the Statistics More than twenty years ago, I interviewed John Faulkner, whose 18-year-old daughter, Jessica, was murdered in May 2004 while attending the University of North Carolina Wilmington. Jessica had been stalked by Curtis Dixon, whose behavior had become increasingly threatening. Her father was left trying to understand why the warning signs had not resulted in the protection she needed. Only weeks later, another UNC Wilmington student, 22-year-old Christen Naujoks, was murdered by a former boyfriend. Christen had sought help and obtained a protective order. It wasn't enough to save her. I have carried those stories with me for more than two decades. One young woman did not know how to get the protection she needed. Another sought protection and still ended up dead. Their families were left with grief that no amount of money or public sympathy could erase. These are the women we are talking about when we discuss domestic violence. They are not simply statistics in an annual report or numbers used to justify another grant application. They are daughters, mothers, sisters, and friends whose lives may depend on whether someone answers the telephone, opens a shelter door, or recognizes the danger before it is too late. That is why organizations such as 1736 Family Crisis Center matter. And it is why their financial decisions deserve scrutiny. The People in the Trenches The staff at 1736 Family Crisis Center spend their working days trying to help save other people's lives, yet some can barely afford to support themselves. These are the people answering crisis calls, finding emergency shelter for women fleeing abusive relationships, comforting traumatized children, and sometimes making decisions that can mean the difference between life and death. They work nights, weekends, and holidays because domestic violence doesn't keep business hours. Yet residential care positions at the organization have been advertised at approximately $20 an hour, or $41,600 annually for a full-time employee before taxes. Try living on that in Los Angeles. Related: He said. He said. End of Story. In November 2022, an employee reviewing the organization on Indeed complained that the wages weren't enough to live on. That was nearly four years ago, before the cost of just about everything went up even further. And the complaints weren't limited to wages. In September 2019, an employee writing on Glassdoor questioned senior management's salaries, encouraged readers to examine the organization's IRS Form 990, and complained that the CEO rarely appeared at the office. Those are allegations from anonymous employee reviews, not independently verified findings. But it's worth considering that employees were raising questions about executive compensation and management's presence seven years before the current controversy. What Does Carol Adelkoff Actually Cost This Charity? According to the organization's IRS Form 990, Adelkoff received $816,023 in reported compensation for fiscal 2025. The previous year, she received $985,552. That's $1,801,575 over two years. Her fiscal 2025 compensation alone was equivalent to the annual earnings of nearly twenty full-time employees making $20 an hour. And we still do not know whether the apartment and vehicle benefits were included in those compensation figures or recorded separately. Meanwhile, the charity has reported operating deficits for three consecutive years: $573,097 in fiscal 2023, $172,704 in fiscal 2024, and $62,260 in fiscal 2025. That's $808,061 in cumulative deficits. Those figures do not establish that executive pay caused the shortfalls, but they do make the board's spending priorities a legitimate subject of inquiry. Then there's Ronald C. Troupe, president of the board of directors, who reportedly received $66,000 annually for approximately 30 hours of work a week. That's $24,400 more than the annual pay of a full-time employee earning $20 an hour. Related: Stay Woke: What My Father Learned About Race in America Paying a nonprofit board member is not automatically improper. But what services does Troupe provide for that money? Who approved his compensation, and how was its reasonableness determined? The board is responsible for overseeing management, not simply signing off on its decisions. Perhaps the board should consider spreading some of that generosity around. Meanwhile, Carol Adelkoff is rolling around Kamuela, on Hawaii's Big Island, in a Beemer leased by the charity. A Charity, Not a Corporation Has anyone at 1736 Family Crisis Center ever heard of the appearance of impropriety? The charity's attorney has characterized the executive apartment as a business expense rather than taxable compensation. Perhaps the arrangement is permissible under IRS rules. But legality and sound judgment are not necessarily the same thing. When nearly 94 percent of an organization's revenue comes from government grants, its board has an obligation to consider more than whether an expense can be justified on paper. It should also consider whether the expenditure is consistent with the organization's mission and the public trust placed in it. The appearance of impropriety alone should have been enough to make the board reconsider. This kind of incongruity says something about the culture of an organization and the priorities of those running it. When a charity's leadership enjoys benefits that seem so far removed from the circumstances of the people it serves, you have to wonder whether its board has lost sight of the very mission it was entrusted to protect. There are legitimate questions about how these arrangements were approved, whether personal benefits were properly accounted for, and whether the expenses were permitted under the organization's government funding agreements. Those questions deserve answers from the board and the agencies providing public money. The Cost of Losing Public Trust People support domestic-violence organizations because they want to help someone escape danger. They picture their contributions paying for a shelter bed, counseling, transportation, or basic necessities for a woman who leaves home with little more than the clothes she is wearing. They do not expect their generosity to be taken for granted. The available records do not establish which funding sources paid for the executive benefits, but that is one more reason to demand an accounting. The last thing I want is for revelations about executive compensation to discourage people from supporting an organization whose services may mean the difference between life and death. The women and families who depend on 1736 Family Crisis Center should not have to pay the price for decisions made in its executive offices. If anything, these revelations should remind us why responsible oversight is so important. The mission deserves our support, and the people entrusted with carrying it out deserve our scrutiny. There's an old saying that charity begins at home. At 1736 Family Crisis Center, someone appears to have taken that personally, and I do mean personally. Eva Amar is a community activist and contributing writer covering land use, development and government accountability in the northwest San Fernando Valley. For more than two decades, she has also advocated for campus sexual-assault victims and for legislation strengthening campus safety, transparency and accountability.

articles.title: Double Standard on War Crimes
articles.author: Marjorie Cohn
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The U.S. government has long sought to incapacitate the International Criminal Court (ICC), the world’s first global court that was created to prosecute the most atrocious crimes. As the ICC seeks to provide accountability for Israeli crimes, the Trump administration has become increasingly aggressive in its attempts to hobble the court. On October 9, 2026, Team Trump imposed punitive sanctions against the court itself, which constitutes the gravest intensification of its war on the ICC. But there are several strategies available to mitigate the worst effects of these sanctions. Executive Order 14203, Signed February 2025 In February 2025, Donald Trump issued Executive Order 14203, which authorizes the imposition of sanctions against the ICC. The sanctions amount to illegal unilateral coercive measures because only the UN Security Council has the authority to impose sanctions. The executive order prohibits U.S. persons from providing material support or services to certain designated persons and entities, including financial services. It exposes non-U.S. persons to secondary sanctions for engaging in conduct prohibited under the order. U.S. persons who violate it may face criminal penalties of up to 20 years imprisonment and fines of up to $1 million. Trump’s 2025 order has led to the sanctioning of nine of the ICC’s 18 judges, three ICC prosecutors, the ICC president, and a senior ICC trial attorney. The Trump administration also sanctioned three highly respected Palestinian human rights organizations — Al-Haq, Al Mezan, and the Palestinian Centre for Human Rights — for their assistance to the ICC. Francesca Albanese , UN Special Rapporteur on Occupied Palestine, who wrote three courageous reports documenting Israel’s genocide in Gaza, was sanctioned as well. The October 9 Sanctions In December 2025, a top Trump administration official told Reuters there was “growing concern” that “the ICC will turn its attention to the president, to the vice president, to the secretary of war and others, and pursue prosecutions against them,” adding that this was “unacceptable, and we will not allow it to happen.” He said the ICC had been warned that unless it amended the Rome Statute to ensure it would not investigate Trump and his top officials, new and very severe U.S. sanctions would be imposed on the court. Sure enough, in an attempt to permanently paralyze the court, the Trump administration sanctioned the entire ICC on October 9, pursuant to Executive Order 14203. These harsh financial sanctions prevent the court from using U.S. dollars and U.S.-based financial services and technology companies. They bar U.S. citizens and companies from supplying the court with funds, goods, or services without a license from the U.S. Treasury. U.S. sanctions have serious impacts on targeted individuals, whose bank accounts can be frozen or closed. Their financial transactions can be rejected, and they can be denied access to digital services and entry into the United States. Sanctions have a chilling effect on non-U.S. banks and other companies outside the jurisdiction of the United States; they themselves could lose access to the U.S. banking system. The ICC could lose access to companies on which it relies for its critical functions, including banking, information, technology, and travel. Although the sanctions contain a six-month wind-down period and exemptions for certain services, they still pose significant risks. In the face of global reliance on the U.S. financial and IT systems, even non-U.S. service providers, including banks, might stop providing services to the ICC for fear of penalties or reprisals by the U.S. Treasury. This could affect the court’s ability to maintain a bank account, receive financial contributions from States Parties, pay staff, make payments, and maintain essential operations. Related: The Most Dangerous Branch? How the Roberts Court Is Reshaping American Democracy The imposition of these outrageous sanctions is the latest, and most devastating, chapter in the U.S.’s long campaign to undermine the ICC. Moreover, these sanctions were imposed on the same day that the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Navi Pillay, a South African lawyer who served as a judge on the ICC for five years and led the UN Commission of Inquiry in 2025 that confirmed Israel’s commission of genocide in Gaza. History of U.S. Attacks on the ICC The International Criminal Court, which became operational in 2002, is a permanent international court created to prosecute individuals for genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity, and the crime of aggression. Nearly two-thirds of the nations in the world have ratified the Rome Statute, thereby becoming States Parties and taking responsibility for arresting and sending those under warrants to the ICC for trial. The court was established to complement, not replace, national criminal justice systems. It will assume jurisdiction only when national systems are unwilling or unable to prosecute. Bill Clinton signed the ICC’s Rome Statute in 2000 as his presidential term was ending, but George W. Bush removed the U.S. signature from it in 2002. The U.S. Congress then enacted the “The Hague Invasion Act,” which says that if a national of the U.S. or its ally (which includes Israel) is detained by the ICC in The Hague, the U.S. military can use armed force to extricate them. The Bush administration effectively blackmailed 100 States Parties to the Rome Statute by forcing them to sign bilateral immunity agreements in which they promised not to turn over U.S. persons to the ICC, or the U.S. would withhold their foreign aid. In November 2024, after an investigation lasting more than three years, the ICC issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant. They stand charged with the war crimes of starvation as a form of warfare, and intentional attacks on civilians; and the crimes against humanity of murder, persecution, and other inhumane acts, for their actions in Gaza since October 7, 2023. The U.S. contends that the ICC has no jurisdiction over Israeli (or U.S.) nationals since neither Israel nor the U.S. are States Parties to the Rome Statute. However, the statute authorizes the ICC to exercise territorial jurisdiction over crimes committed by non-State Party nationals in the territory of a State Party. Palestine is a State Party to the statute, so the ICC determined that it has jurisdiction over crimes allegedly committed by Israeli nationals in Palestine. Indeed, the U.S. has supported several ICC investigations and prosecutions of crimes allegedly committed by non-State Party nationals, including the arrest warrant that the court issued for Russian President Vladimir Putin . On July 13, 2026, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio pledged to “dismantle” the International Criminal Court. He accused the ICC of “waging a war against our country, not with bullets or missiles,” but with “the force of so-called international law.” Venezuela and Chad announced their withdrawal from the Rome Statute following U.S. threats to reduce or withdraw assistance if they refused to do so. Related: The 2026 Midterms May Not End on Election Day Meanwhile, the court faces a leadership vacuum following the firing in July 2026 of the ICC’s former chief prosecutor Karim Khan, who had requested the issuance of the arrest warrants against Netanyahu and Gallant. UN investigators said they “found evidence that Mr. Khan engaged in ‘non-consensual sexual contact’” with a lawyer who had worked as a special assistant to him in 2023. But after a three-month review of a 152-page report by the Office of Internal Oversight Services and of the 5,000+ pages of underpinning material, the Ad Hoc Panel of Judicial Experts unanimously determined that the facts did not establish evidence beyond a reasonable doubt of any wrongdoing on the part of Khan. Nevertheless, the Assembly of States Parties to the Rome Statute voted to fire him with no due process on July 24. In December 2026, the assembly will elect six judges to fill one-third of the ICC’s 18 judicial seats. The U.S. will invariably endeavor to interfere with those elections. Lawsuits Challenging EO 14203 On July 15, Democracy for the Arab World Now and the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, alleging that Trump’s EO 14203 violates the constitutional right to engage in Palestine-related human rights advocacy. They claimed that the sanctions violate the First Amendment by limiting what people in the U.S. can say to an international tribunal or to foreign advocates, and by limiting their ability to associate with sanctioned parties. U.S. District Judge Jesse M. Furman granted Democracy for the Arab World Now and the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide a temporary restraining order on October 13, which temporarily blocks the Trump administration from imposing civil or criminal penalties on the two organizations for supporting ICC’s investigations into alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. The judge said the two organizations were likely to prevail on their claims that Trump’s sanctions violated the First Amendment. Democracy for the Arab World Now announced it would immediately resume its advocacy with the ICC for the prosecution of Israeli and U.S. perpetrators of grave crimes, and it will work with the three sanctioned human rights groups and the Special Rapporteur. On August 11, the American Friends Service Committee, the Center for Constitutional Rights, Human Rights Watch, and the Open Society Institute filed a lawsuit in the same New York federal court, alleging that Trump’s executive order violates the U.S. Constitution; U.S. statutes; and international law, including the Genocide Convention, Geneva Conventions, and customary international law. Actions to Protect the ICC On October 12, the Coalition for the International Criminal Court (CICC), comprised of more than 120 organizations from over 60 countries representing all regions of the world, and dozens of legal experts, human rights defenders, and members of the EU, issued a joint statement , urging States Parties to act now to protect the ICC from unlawful U.S. sanctions. The statement condemned “unequivocally and in the strongest terms the decision by the United States to impose unlawful sanctions on the International Criminal Court.” The CICC said, “This unprecedented measure represents a direct attack against the rule of law, the independence of the Court and international justice, ultimately undermining the rights of millions of victims and survivors of mass atrocities worldwide.” The CICC listed 12 actions that States Parties should take, individually and collectively, to protect the court. They include the immediate adoption or activation of blocking measures at the national and regional levels; for example, the immediate adoption of the EU Blocking Statute and equivalent domestic legislation elsewhere. Blocking measures would shield those sanctioned, including the court and its officials, the UN Special Rapporteur, and civil society organizations, from the extraterritorial reach of the sanctions. Related: Trump's Pro-Israel EO 14203 Receives Fierce Pushback In addition, the CICC urges States Parties to guarantee that the court and those cooperating with it have access to banking and other essential services; to find concrete measures to mitigate the impact of sanctions on civic space, freedom of speech, and freedom of association; and to explore all possible diplomatic and legal avenues to challenge the sanctions and their legality under international law, including by supporting U.S. legal challenges and a referral to the International Court of Justice. And the CICC implores States Parties to refuse, “without exception,” coercion by a non-State Party to influence votes, positions, or conduct within the Assembly of States Parties or any other body of the Rome Statute system. The battle to save the ICC and its capacity to enforce accountability for the most heinous crimes is one struggle with many fronts: local, regional, national, and international. TruthOut

articles.title: Jacobin Is International
articles.author: Asher Dupuy-Spencer
articles.content: Jacobin began in the United States, but our emancipatory project has always been internationalist. The questions we’re focused on — about who holds power in our societies, about how capitalism shapes our lives, and how working people can abolish class society — extend across borders. Alongside our English-language magazine, Jacobin publishes regularly in six other languages: Dutch: Jacobin Nederland Greek: Jacobin Greece German: Jacobin Magazin Italian: Jacobin Italia Portuguese: Jacobin Brasil , based in Brazil Spanish: Jacobin América Latina , based in Argentina We’re also working on launching editions in French, Romanian, and Urdu. We’ll share more as those projects develop. Building a socialist left means learning from struggles everywhere, and it means exchanges at a more theoretical level with Marxists around the world. Our international editions play an important role in fostering those connections and combating the parochialism that has long plagued progressive milieus in the United States. If you read any of these languages, take a look at the editions linked above. And if you know someone who might be interested, send one their way. And if you’d like to support our work coordinating these networks, please consider subscribing or visiting jacobin.com/donate/ to learn about tax-deductible donations to our project. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. Subscribe to the print edition for $20 a year.

articles.title: The Video Game Industry’s Crisis Is a Crisis of Capitalism
articles.author: Alexandre Paquet
articles.content: Montreal has been touted as a major creative hub for the video game industry for over twenty years, leading the province of Quebec’s efforts to develop its digital creative sector. The industry reportedly generates CAD$1.4 billion in annual revenues within the province, yet game workers feel the lack of job security more than ever. At the end of the summer, games workers rallied in Montreal to support the Bethesda employees affected by recent layoffs. Back in July, Microsoft announced it was eliminating 3,200 jobs within the Xbox division before the end of the year. Among the employees affected is Simon Préfontaine, a designer with over nine years under his belt at Bethesda Montreal. He explains that layoffs have become an annual occurrence across Xbox studios and the industry more broadly. What does worker power look like in an industry where the people making the games often have little control over whether their jobs, studios, or projects survive? According to Préfontaine, “People are now much more motivated and radicalized. We are ready to strike. [These companies have] pissed these people off enough.” There seems to be a growing sentiment among game workers in Montreal that organizing themselves and unionizing their workplace is becoming necessary. At the heart of Montreal’s game industry, there is a familiar contradiction of capitalism: while workers collectively produce value through their labor power, corporate owners privately control that value. The video game industry exemplifies this contradiction. The people who make the games own very little of what they produce while bearing all the risks. But how did Montreal become such a hub in the first place? The Crisis for Quebecois Video Game Workers Is the Crisis Everywhere The turning point can be traced back to 1997, when Ubisoft established a video game studio in the city. As Sylvianne Pilon and Diane-Gabrielle Tremblay note in their study of video game clusters, there were multiple converging factors leading to this development, such as the city’s strong digital animation culture and its pool of creative talent. But most important of all was Quebec government policy, which subsidized the employer’s wage bill. A 2020 study found that public support included a 30 percent labor tax credit, amounting to about $100 million per year. What followed was a flourishing of the industry, according to La Guilde du jeu vidéo du Québec, a nonprofit cooperative that brings together members of the video game industry. Electronic Arts Montreal was established in 2004, Eidos-Montréal in 2007, and a wide range of independent developers followed. Quebec, and Montreal in particular, became the hub it is today. If this industry is growing, then why are game workers feeling such pressure? Precarity is at an all-time high, and layoffs occur constantly, sapping the morale of workers already struggling to remain afloat. As Préfontaine puts it, “They’re asking you to give 110 percent, but they’re not even going to give you thirteen months without making you worry [about your job]. It’s very difficult.” What Préfontaine describes is not an isolated incident or a specific case of targeted layoffs at Bethesda Montreal. Rather, it is part of the general experience of workers who bear the brunt when capitalism’s recurring crises hit. As Eric Cazdyn puts it when describing crisis within capitalism in The Already Dead : “Crisis is not what happens when we go wrong; crisis is what happens when we go right.” Crisis, in other words, is built into the system itself. The widespread layoffs affecting the industry over the past three-plus years seem, once again, to confirm this point. Workers organizing in the video game industry are at a disadvantage due to the industry being fragmented across studios, projects, contract types, and national borders. Further, the industry has long relied on the culture of “passion work.” As Carolyn Jong from Game Workers Unite Montreal explains, “It is a very passion-oriented industry. And that is used as a vehicle for justifying a lot of exploitation and poor working conditions.” Jamie Woodcock, a senior lecturer at King’s College London and member of the Game Worker Solidarity Project , identifies an apparent paradox of the industry: despite its enormous profitability, it is repeatedly hit by layoffs. “The reality is that capital doesn’t care about making games. The interest of capital is about extracting surplus value from the production of games. [This crisis is] not a bug.” These conditions help explain why collective organization has proved so difficult for game workers in spite of the example set by established trade unions. Leveling Up to Fight the Boss While the historical decline of unions under neoliberalism is well documented , Woodcock argues that this is less the result of the disappearance of existing unions than of a failure to unionize new sectors of the economy. Companies have worked hard to convince people that unions are unnecessary or harmful while also engaging in union-busting practices the push the boundaries of legality. A recent example is Rockstar Games’ termination of thirty-four employees, widely suspected of being a union-busting initiative. Yet the reality might not be as grim as it seems. In fact, Woodcock suggests that, when compared to trade unions, which took decades to organize, the video game industry is actually progressing very quickly. “Over the past seven years, we have seen unions go from effectively nonexistent to having unions at some of the largest video games companies,” he explains. Thinking back on the beginnings of Game Workers Unite Montreal’s efforts to organize workers within the city, Jong mentions that an early challenge was the lack of knowledge about unions and how to even begin to organize. It took some time to change the way workers in the industry thought about their relationship to their work. In fact, “the instinct to self-identify as a worker wasn’t really there,” she says. Game worker organizing has progressed considerably since 2018, when the Montreal unit of Game Workers Unite launched. The organization now supports workers across multiple studios, providing resources, materials, workshops, and more. They played a big part in supporting the August 18 rally for Bethesda workers, for example. They also provide a platform for cross-studio organizing within the city as well as bridge between the local realities of Montreal and the global network of game workers worldwide. Bethesda Montreal was the first studio to formally unionize in Quebec back in 2024 . However, unionization did not stop Microsoft’s subsequent layoffs. Préfontaine’s experience illustrates the limits of what a union can do. Although often incapable of preventing an employer from cutting jobs, unions can give workers a collective voice over the process and help secure contractual protections. But, as Jong argues, it would be a mistake to judge unions solely by whether they can avert any particular round of layoffs. Their broader value lies in the possibilities arising from an organized workforce. As Woodcock puts it, “labor unions are the vehicle through which workers can fight in the workplace against capital.” On this view, developing an alternative conception and practice of work requires struggle in the workplace — struggle that unions can organize and sustain. “Struggle is also pedagogical. If we can’t learn to fight in our own workplace, then the chance that we can take on a capitalist government or capital is vanishingly unlikely,” he adds. Unions can improve wages and conditions, negotiate severance, and give workers a collective voice. But their importance extends far beyond this. They also provide institutions through which to develop the knowledge, resources, and practices needed to confront the volatility that capitalism inflicts on them. Such gains may not be immediately apparent, but they remain vital for creating a more confident and politically capable working class. Workers’ Tales Woodcock notes that game workers need a “a unionized sector that tells stories about unionization.” This is how both workers and the public can come to see unionization not only as possible but as a source of tangible workplace gains. In Montreal, game workers collectively produce games that generate enormous cultural and economic value. Yet control over employment, investment, and ownership remains largely in the hands of local and multinational corporations. Unions can provide workers with a collective voice and the means to push back in times of crisis, even when the results fall short of what they hope for. Préfontaine encourages all game workers to reach out to Game Workers Unite and other organizations supporting unionization initiatives. Looking back on his own involvement in Bethesda Montreal’s unionization efforts and recent layoff, he states: “I do not regret anything.” Workers may not be able to stop the next layoff on their own, but, organized together, they can begin to build the power to resist not only the next round of cuts but the system that makes those cuts inevitable. articles.title: Anwar Shaikh Changed My Life
articles.author: E. Ahmet Tonak
articles.content: Anwar Shaikh, one of the most important Marxist economists of his generation, died on October 6 at the age of eighty in New York City. Two years ago, a conference was held to mark his retirement from the Department of Economics at the New School for Social Research, where he had taught for fifty years. I was one of the speakers on the first panel. I opened my talk by adapting the famous first line of Orhan Pamuk’s Yeni Hayat ( The New Life ), knowing that Pamuk was one of Anwar’s favorite writers: “I met Anwar Shaikh, and my whole life changed!” That is truly what happened. After the 1971 military coup in Turkey, I went first to Sweden and then came to the United States. While doing political organizing with Turkish students in New York, I was also trying to finish a master’s degree in applied mathematics and statistics, partly to keep myself occupied. My plan was to return home at the first opportunity and work as a journalist, inspired by the politically exhilarating days I had spent at the newspaper Yeni Ortam in the early 1970s. By then I had married, and when complications over my military service obligations made it necessary for me to stay in the United States a while longer, I began looking into the doctoral program in Marxist economics at the New School. That’s where, in 1975, I first met Anwar in his office. He was very warm toward me and strongly encouraged me to apply to the program. I think our immediate rapport came from the fact that he had lived in Turkey as a child, and that I had a background in engineering and mathematics. In the doctoral program, I not only took all of Anwar’s courses but also became his first paid teaching and research assistant. His research helped me settle on my dissertation topic, which eventually led to the book we wrote together. In short, my life really did change. I had met Anwar, and instead of returning to Turkey to pursue journalism, I found myself drawn into economics and, eventually, an academic career. Anything written in memory of someone who taught for fifty years — a man who left behind thousands of pages of published work and thousands of files of unpublished notes, letters, and other materials, and made contributions not just to one field of economics but to nearly all of them — will inevitably be selective. I want to touch briefly on two concepts that Anwar pioneered and on how they inspired me and a later generation of researchers to pursue new lines of inquiry. Anwar’s unpublished 1975 paper, “IO Accounts and Marxian Categories,” and his famous 1978 paper, “National Income Accounts and Marxian Categories,” which circulated from hand to hand almost like samizdat, can be considered early drafts of Measuring the Wealth of Nations , the book we eventually published together in 1994. The 1978 paper contains a preliminary calculation of net tax (taxes on labor income minus expenditures on labor income) covering just three years. This category aimed to show how the capitalist state’s distributional policies affected productive workers and altered the rate of surplus value. In my dissertation, I extended these calculations to cover 1952 to 1980, again using the net tax category. Later, in two papers on the subject, Anwar and I replaced net tax with the category of net social wage (expenditures on labor income minus taxes on labor income) and questioned whether a welfare state could really be said to exist in the United States. Today there is a substantial body of literature on the net social wage in various countries, including Turkey. My younger colleague Yakup Karabacak and I recently completed the most comprehensive of the Turkish studies, contributing once again to a field of research that Anwar had opened up. Let me now turn to profit on alienation (POA), a concept that Anwar began using in the 1970s in the context of the transformation problem and that later appeared both in our joint book, Measuring the Wealth of Nations , and in his 2016 magnum opus, Capitalism: Competition, Conflict, Crises . Marxists have generally been reluctant to embrace this concept. After all, under capitalism, the fundamental source of profit is surplus value generated in the sphere of production, while profit on alienation is discussed in the Marxist literature mainly in connection with precapitalist merchant profit. Yet as my former student Alper Duman and I tried to show in a paper we wrote together, POA also provides a useful starting point for analyzing phenomena within capitalism itself: both privatizations, which have been central to neoliberal policies, and the gains banks extract from workers’ incomes. In that paper, we also sought to operationalize the concept in the Turkish context and estimate it empirically. In a sense, following in Anwar’s footsteps, we gave concrete empirical form to a concept whose importance he had emphasized primarily at the theoretical level. Since Anwar’s death, social media posts and written tributes have come mostly from American academic circles, particularly his colleagues and his current and former students. Most, like this one, recall the parts of his work and character that shaped their authors. For me, one of the most remarkable tributes is the personal account of Wando Frank. Frank wrote about how Anwar’s writings had also changed the course of his life: I won’t pretend I didn’t tear up seeing this. I remember working the backshift in Dover, a petrol pump factory, and trying to read Anwar’s excellent book Capitalism in the canteen on my break one night. Whilst I understood the gist of his arguments, it was far too technical in places for me. I was determined that I wouldn’t be defeated and would learn to understand the work. Six months later I applied to go to Dundee University to study Economics, which gave me enough of a basic grounding in statistics to grapple with the book. It became my go-to point of reference for most essays. Any essay I wrote utilising this book was marked first class. Being able to reconstruct his study of American inflation in the British context was one of the most rewarding things I have ever had the privilege to do. We both showed that in the USA, and in Britain, Marx was completely right about inflation and the central bankers were completely wrong. Without Anwar, I would not have a first-class honours degree, and that’s just a fact. Without Anwar, I would not have the life I have today either. And that’s a fact too. articles.title: Tax the Rich and Slash the Military Budget
articles.author: Nancy Folbre
articles.content: Here’s a question progressives get asked constantly: Fine, you want universal childcare, Medicare for All, and a green economy — but how are you going to pay for it? As part of the Game Changers project , economists Gerald Epstein and Aaron Medlin just answered it with a full accounting. They price out the thirty policies in the Game Changers initiative and show, line by line, how to fund them without adding a dime to the deficit — by taxing wealth and capital the same way the United States already taxes wages and by shrinking a military and immigration-enforcement budget that is both bloated and destructive. The burden of the increased taxes they propose would fall most heavily on those in the upper reaches of the top 1 percent. The Underlying Problem Let’s start with the scale of inequality that these thirty policy proposals are responding to. The top 1 percent of American households hold about a third of the nation’s wealth and roughly half of the stock market. In income terms, that same 1 percent takes home twice as much as the entire bottom half of the country combined. The effects ripple outward: stagnant demand drags down growth, upward mobility stalls, and a small elite ends up with political influence wildly out of proportion to its numbers. Meanwhile, ordinary families get squeezed from both sides — wages haven’t kept pace with productivity, and housing, health care, and childcare keep getting more expensive. At the same time, advances in AI threaten to make even stable jobs feel precarious. Epstein and Medlin’s sharper point is that this isn’t just about how wealth is distributed — it’s about how the government pays its bills. The way Washington currently finances itself is a driver of inequality. Labor income gets taxed heavily and reliably; wealth and capital income get taxed lightly and unevenly. Whatever isn’t collected gets borrowed instead — mostly from the same wealthy households who weren’t taxed for it, who then collect interest on the loan, year after year. It’s a system that manufactures inequality twice: once by under-taxing fortunes, and then again by paying those fortunes interest on the resulting debt. The numbers back this up. Between 2018 and 2020, the four hundred richest Americans paid an average tax rate of about 24 percent on their pretax income — lower than what the bottom 50 percent of income earners pay on average, and far below the 45 percent top labor-income earners pay. Since two-thirds of federal bonds, which the government issues to borrow money, are held by private investors, interest payments flow disproportionately to people who are already wealthy. The result: the four hundred richest Americans held about $300 billion (in today’s dollars) in 1982; by 2025 that amount had grown more than twentyfold, to $6.6 trillion. Republican administrations from Ronald Reagan’s through both Donald Trump terms accelerated federal government borrowing with tax cuts skewed to the top. Most recently, the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which the Congressional Budget Office projects will cut federal revenue by trillions and widen the deficit by roughly $3–4 trillion through 2034, will hand the richest 1 percent over $50,000 a year in tax cuts. Meanwhile, revenue from the corporate income tax, which taxes corporate profits, has collapsed from 7 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1944 to about 1 percent in 2019. As Warren Buffett famously put it , an economy where his receptionist pays a higher tax rate than he does “does not strike me as a just economy.” The authors are careful to note that deficits aren’t inherently bad — borrowing to fund productive investment (such as education, infrastructure, and most of the Game Changers agenda) pays for itself over time because the social return exceeds the cost. The danger is borrowing to fund waste: excess military spending, fossil fuel subsidies, and corporate giveaways. That kind of borrowing doesn’t just fail to pay off — it deepens inequality and, if debt costs ever outrun economic growth, can become self-reinforcing. The Plan: Tax Capital Like Labor, Cut Wasteful Spending So, what’s the fix? The Game Changers policies are split into three funding categories. Many need no new government money at all — things like stronger labor protections, national rent control, fairer trade rules, or a four-day workweek, which change laws and norms rather than spend cash. A second group has dedicated funding mechanisms tied to the programs themselves: polluters fund climate resilience and a fossil fuel phasedown; scaled premiums fund paid family leave, disaster insurance, and long-term care. Medicare for All, the single biggest item, mostly falls into this category too — it eliminates private insurance premiums, leaving most Americans paying less overall and only the wealthiest paying more. A third group of policies — universal childcare, a child allowance, social housing, plus a small residual slice of Medicare for All — requires general tax revenue. That’s the piece this brief is really about, and the plan pays for it two ways. First, spending gets reallocated by cutting military spending deemed unnecessary for genuine defense and shrinking Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s budget in favor of a more humane immigrant-integration system. Together, these reallocations free up between $208 billion and $413 billion a year. Second, a new revenue package targets the income that goes untaxed or is under-taxed by the current tax code: capital gains, corporate profits, inherited fortunes, and speculative trading, rather than paychecks. Concretely, that means restoring the corporate tax rate from the current rate of 21 percent to 35 percent (its pre-2017 level, falling mostly on roughly 350 highly profitable firms); raising the corporate minimum tax from 15 percent to 21 percent of taxable profits; quadrupling the stock buyback tax (charging corporations when they repurchase their own stock) from 1 percent to 4 percent; funding serious Internal Revenue Service enforcement against wealthy tax avoidance; adding a small financial-transactions tax on trades of stocks, bonds, and other securities; creating a minimum income tax on total income for households worth over $100 million; and eliminating the loophole that lets inherited wealth escape capital gains tax entirely when it changes hands at death. Crucially, wages are taxed in a progressive way, with households earning less than $20,000 paying no wage taxes at all, and even households earning as much as $200,000 paying less overall once lower health costs, the child allowance, and federally funded childcare are taken into account. The bulk of the tax burden would land at the top. Does the Math Work? Yes, with room to spare. Subtracting the military and ICE savings from the cost of programs that require general funding, the needed funds come to between $557.3 billion and $614.3 billion. The revenue package raises between $701.8 billion and $1.425 trillion, exceeding the general revenue requirement by approximately $87.5 billion to $868 billion. Epstein and Medlin are careful to call this one workable combination among many, not the only path — and they note their estimates are conservative, since many Game Changers policies (healthier kids, cheaper health care, fewer financial crises, and avoided climate damage) would likely pay for themselves in ways the brief doesn’t even count. Their larger argument is that funding a fairer economy and shrinking inequality aren’t competing goals requiring trade-offs. They’re the same project, since concentrated wealth left untaxed doesn’t just distort the budget: it buys the political power to keep itself that way. articles.title: The Political Economy of the Restaurant
articles.author: Ed Luker
articles.content: English food does not have a good reputation. In 1806, Grimod de La Reynière, a pioneering French food critic, wrote that “[England’s] cooking is limited to boiled chickens.” More than two hundred years later, stereotypes about the country’s food have hardly improved. Looking at the staple icons of English cuisine today — fish and chips, the Sunday roast, the full English breakfast — one might agree with Grimod’s point. These dishes are brutish mounds of meat and carbs, the product of a culture that has often seemed more interested in excess than culinary refinement. They hardly suggest the level of technique and attention to simple, high-quality ingredients associated with French or Japanese food. It’s not only the nation’s cuisine that’s in a sorry state. Ultraprocessed food accounts for more than half of the calories consumed in the UK each year, while obesity rates remain substantially higher than the European Union average. How did England come to eat this way? In his first book, The Full English: The Ways We Eat and Why , the chef and writer Lewis Bassett examines the country’s culinary traditions and eating habits in order to understand the peculiar history that produced them. Making a loaf of sourdough in a North London bakery, learning how to cook a balti in a Birmingham curry house, fishing off the shores of Eastbourne: the reader follows Bassett as he improves his technique and expands his repertoire of “English” dishes — a category that is distinctly more multicultural than its marketing suggests. Loosely, the book is structured around a series of stages (from stagiaire , the French term for a professional kitchen internship), with each placement and dish giving Bassett another vantage point from which to investigate English society. He not only moves between restaurants but also across roles, switching from worker to reporter and researcher. Bassett began working in kitchens at sixteen, first making sandwiches before shucking oysters and frying burgers in Melbourne at eighteen; at twenty, he worked in a London fish restaurant where he was taught how to cook professionally. His other education was political. During the Jeremy Corbyn years he became involved in the Labour left, undertaking grassroots organizing and campaigning while completing a PhD at the University of Manchester on Corbynism and democracy under neoliberalism. He has since written about politics and organizing for this publication and others. Cooking and socialist organizing became two different forms of education. As a chef working in London, Bassett has cooked for some of the wealthiest people in the world. As a socialist, he lives in a society in which access to good food made from fresh ingredients remains profoundly uneven. The book is situated inside the tensions that emerge when you do something you truly love in an exclusionary industry. After completing his PhD, and during the pandemic, the culinary work on which the book draws was an attempt to return to what Bassett calls “the careful, physical work that is done with human hands.” What the hands do, the brain wants to understand. The Full English uses the practical knowledge of cooking as the starting point for an investigation into the particular development of British society, its early industrialization, and its imperial expansion. The world of gourmet restaurants depends upon a mostly hidden system of large and highly specialized teams. Behind a Michelin-starred meal are chefs carrying out exacting, repetitive tasks at speed: tweezing fragments of shell from crab meat, slicing paper-thin sheets of apple with a mandolin, coordinating dozens of preparations at the peak of service. The refinement associated with haute cuisine can obscure the conditions required to produce it. Luxury arrives at the table looking effortless only because so much effort has been organized elsewhere, through an intense division of labor. The same tension between refinement and material conditions can be seen in something as ordinary as bread. Sourdough is often treated as a return to an older, more authentic way of eating, yet the highly standardized loaf made from carefully controlled ingredients is product of modern abundance. In preindustrial England, bread was necessarily more of a motley affair, made from whatever grains or substitutes were available, sometimes including peas, and fermented with beer rather than a modern sourdough starter. Industrialization has made food more uniform and predictable; that consumable standardization has helped create the middle-class boom in desire for the artisanal and handcrafted. What looks like a rejection of industrial food is, in part, one of its consequences, one that exists for consumers who want to pay to feel like they’re opting out. English eating habits were transformed unusually early by urbanization and industrialization. Through dispossession and the consolidation of land, England lost much of its peasantry earlier than other European countries. By the middle of the nineteenth century, it was already heavily urbanized, with large numbers of people buying bread rather than baking it themselves. The dishes that people ate were shaped by the new rhythms of industrial life. At the same time, British naval and commercial power opened up new systems of trade and consumption. English taste emerged from this “peculiar insistence of modernity,” as Bassett puts it: industrial, urban, and imperial all at the same time. The later sections of The Full English move outward from the kitchen into questions of class, migration, and national identity. The Balti, a Pakistani curry, becomes a way of thinking about the anglicization of so-called South Asian food and the colonial histories behind it; Italian food, meanwhile, is tied to the rise of a new middle class in the 1990s and the cultural politics of New Labour. Elsewhere, the language of dieting and optimization enters the kitchen through food alternatives like Huel and calorie-counting apps, turning eating into another activity to be measured and disciplined. This is perhaps the least surprising part of the book: the critique of neoliberal self-management is familiar even if the examples themselves are revealing. More compelling is the way these examples accumulate into a history of how English tastes have been shaped by empire, class formation, and changing ideas of aspiration. The investigations in the book become most politically urgent when they turn to land. Britain remains dependent on food imports, while the shocks of war, trade disruptions, and rising prices have shown the fragility of the food system. Yet huge swaths of the countryside remain concentrated in the hands of a landed aristocracy, with estates able to attract public money for heritage and wild-farming projects. At the very moment when questions of food security and agricultural production are becoming harder to ignore, the ownership of land itself is often treated as beyond political discussion. The environmental stewardship of heritage projects can therefore be a way of modernizing the image of inherited wealth without disturbing the structure beneath it. The more radical questions, such as who should own land, what it should produce, and whether farming should be organized around national need rather than market return, remain largely outside respectable debate. The tension between luxury, labor, and poverty runs through the book. There is something almost peripatetic about its movement between kitchens, farms, and fisheries, as though the act of working itself were generating the argument, and we were listening to Bassett talk at his prep station. Cooking is treated neither as pure pleasure nor simply as exploitation. It is skilled, exhausting, communal, and often badly paid; it can also produce extraordinary things that remain inaccessible to much of the population. The core political problem is the access to and distribution of good food. Why should refinement, abundance, and pleasure be restricted to those who can afford them? That question is how The Full English uses food to raise questions of broader political significance. For many socialists of Bassett’s generation, the defeat of Corbynism left open the question of where political energies and intellectual habits might go next. One answer offered here is to return to work to apprenticeship and to the material world, and to produce knowledge from those experiences. There is an older leftist tradition behind this: the self-education of industrial workers, or E. P. Thompson teaching adults outside the university, in which political understanding is produced by immersing yourself in a life built around other workers. The Full English belongs, however loosely, to that tradition. It turns the experience of work into a way of telling stories about the nation and makes food a means of asking who Britain is organized for.
